entries.title: Trump Says Donalds and Moody Called to Ask Him to Approve Florida Hurricane Funding
entries.summary: The Florida Republicans “call up. …They’re always looking for money,” the president said of what triggered the approval of two tranches of disaster relief.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday he approved $184 million in additional FEMA hurricane relief for Florida’s Panhandle a day earlier at the request of two Republicans on the state’s ballot.

“They call up. They bug me all the time. They’re always looking for money,” Trump said, describing requests from Rep. Byron Donalds and Sen. Ashley Moody. “So they call me twice. I said, ‘Listen, just tell them I’m not in.’”

“I don’t know what it is with the Panhandle. I get 98 percent of the vote,” Trump said. “It’s like the most incredible thing.”

He added: “What happened? It rained a little bit. There was a little drizzle. And I gave it to them.”

The money is meant to help individuals affected by Hurricane Isaias, which hit Northwest Florida Oct. 6-12. The funding covers grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-interest loans for uninsured property losses and other recovery programs. The Category 2 storm killed at least four people and left hundreds of thousands without power.

Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor, told the crowd before Trump took the stage that he had asked the president for the money by phone Thursday.

“We need the sign-off for individual assistance from FEMA for the people in the Panhandle,” Donalds said he told Trump. Trump told him it was done, Donalds said. “And it was signed off two hours later for the people in the Panhandle.”

Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis requested a major disaster declaration Oct. 15, seeking public assistance for 15 counties and individual assistance for eight. Federal Emergency Management Agency records show the public assistance request was approved Oct. 27. Trump amended the declaration two days later to include individual assistance for the eight counties.

Approved disaster relief timelines have varied under Trump. FEMA records list 13 declaration requests in process as of this week. Four of them filed before Florida’s are still pending — including August requests from Indiana and Nebraska and September requests from Kansas and Washington. Several others are appeals of earlier denials.

FEMA and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

While he didn’t tie Florida’s disaster relief to the outcome of Tuesday’s elections, Trump has said in campaign stops across the country that Republican losses in the state where he was stumping could cost them federal money.

At a rally in Park City, Kansas, earlier this month, he said if Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton won the Senate seat, he would withhold a fuel waiver.

“I also gave Kansas a waiver to sell E15 all year round. And with Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent,” Trump said. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it.”

Trump tied Camp Lejeune water contamination settlements to Republican control of Congress during a campaign event at Pitt-Greenville Airport in North Carolina.

“If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible,” he said, adding later: “If we don’t win, there’s no money. If we do win, you’re getting it.”

In September, at a rally in Gastonia, North Carolina, Trump said the state was awaiting additional Hurricane Helene funding beyond the $2 billion already spent. “Now if Michael loses, I’m not sending it, OK?” he said, referring to Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley, before adding: “No, I’m only kidding. You’re getting it.”

Earlier in the week, it looked like Friday’s Daytona stop might have been Trump’s last in-person rally of the election following the cancellation of weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa. But less than a day after they were canceled in favor of closing-stretch tele-rallies, the Kansas and Iowa events were rescheduled for Sunday.
entries.author: Ayah Ali-Ahmad

entries.title: A Super PAC Army Is Spending Millions on ‘Spoiler’ Candidates
entries.summary: Congressional hopefuls with little hope have been surprised by the sudden help from shadowy sources.
entries.content:
Last week, a tsunami of outside spending surged onto Bill Redpath’s ultra-longshot campaign for Ohio’s U.S. Senate seat.

A single super PAC created in early October began spending $1.7 million in support of the little-known libertarian, who’s on the ballot alongside Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted and Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown.

In four days, the group spent more than 35 times more on Redpath than the candidate’s own campaign had spent on him for the entire campaign, according to Federal Election Commission data.

“Tired of professional swamp politicians wasting your tax dollars? Vote Redpath for U.S. Senate,” a booming voice says in a digital ad from the super PAC, called Buckeye Freedom PAC. “Both parties suck. Vote for the real conservative.”

Despite this right-wing messaging, the super PAC had hired a vendor exclusively used at the federal level by other PACs boosting outsider candidates — one of which was funded by a liberal dark-money group.

“I agree that both parties suck,” Redpath told The Washington Sun, clarifying that he’s conservative on the economy but "generally not on social issues.” The super PAC, he surmised, is “trying to reach certain people to convince them that I am more aligned with their views; and in some cases, that’s going to be true.”

Redpath’s unexpected super PAC windfall is no anomaly.

In the past two weeks, a collection of super PACs have together spent more than $15 million boosting outsider congressional candidates with little chance of winning — but who could peel enough votes away from the Republican or Democratic candidate to sway the election, according to a Sun analysis.

Voters won’t learn who’s bankrolling many of the outside spending groups until after the election. That’s because the last financial disclosure reports due to the FEC before Election Day cover super PAC financials only up to Oct. 14, and some of these super PACs reported no income prior to that date.

However, The Sun determined — by analyzing their vendors, spending patterns and one-sided attacks on major-party candidates — that many of these super PACs supporting obscure, independent or minor-party candidates had strong ties to Republicans or Democrats.

Some of the relationships between the PACs and partisan organizations have been described in other media outlets.

Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the Campaign Legal Center, said so-called “pop-up” super PACs that materialize right before an election seem to be more common this cycle.

“It’s obviously something we've seen in prior elections, and it points to a very intentional and deliberate approach of denying voters transparency about the true source of the money that's being spent to influence them,” Ghosh said.

Secret Money and Motivations

Pop-up super PACs spending big during the final days of the 2026 election aren’t always what they seem to be. Some appear to have taken extra steps to obscure their motivations and the moneyed forces behind them.

Buckeye Freedom PAC, for its part, paid $50,000 for text messages in support of Redpath.

To do so, it used a firm called Liberty Buying Partners LLC, whose internet presence was limited to a website without a phone number or email on its homepage. The company deleted its website altogether recently after The Sun requested comment.

One of Liberty Buying Partners’ other clients is a super PAC known as Right for Alaska, which had been supporting obscure conservative candidates despite being funded by the Sixteen Thirty Fund, a nonprofit that supports “progressive changemakers,” according to its website.

Right for Alaska terminated its operations in October. But at the same time, two new super PACs popped up in Alaska — and both also use Liberty Buying Partners and the same treasurer.

In Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, Alaska Values PAC is now asking voters to support Republican Gerald Heikes and ditch incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in the race where 16 different candidates appear on the general election ballot.

Heikes decided to run for office after a meeting with a man whose name he could not remember, The New York Times reported Wednesday. Heikes recalled the man telling him that, while he and his associates could not directly donate to Heikes’ campaign, “we’ll make things happen for you,” the Times reported.

Heikes had previously said God called him to run for office.

Neither Buckeye Freedom nor Alaska Values have responded to The Sun’s questions on their intentions or why they chose to work with Liberty Buying Partners.

To Ghosh, this scenario shouldn’t be possible. He suggested that super PACs should be required by law to disclose their major donors on a rolling basis in the days leading up to Election Day, just as candidates’ own committees must.

The current system “leaves a solid two weeks of, essentially, free-for-all,” Ghosh said. “It's really an indictment of Congress that even the most low-hanging fruit of campaign finance reform that would actually really improve transparency right around an election — even that they can’t do.”

Boosting Ooutsiders

In Nevada, Nevadans for Sensible Government has spent $6,000 so far on digital advertising supporting Lynn Chapman, a member of the Independent American Party, in the state’s 2nd Congressional District, where Republican David Flippo and Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson are vying for the historically Republican open seat.

Chapman’s platform is decidedly conservative. But Nevadans for Sensible Government has created its pro-Chapman ad through Pendulum Creative Group, a firm that advertises winning “campaigns for Democratic candidates and progressive organizations,” according to its website.

In Iowa, Our Heritage Matters PAC — established this month — has dropped hundreds of thousands of dollars boosting libertarian U.S. Senate candidate Thomas Laehn, according to FEC data.

Recent polls on the race have Laehn bringing in anywhere from 1% to 8% of the vote — sometimes larger than the pre-election polling margins separating Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek.

It’s unclear who’s funding Our Heritage Matters PAC. But the Iowa GOP says it’s convinced Democrats are behind it — Democrats are “so desperate to win that they’re deploying dark-money groups to boost Libertarian candidates,” Jade Cichy, a spokesperson for the Iowa GOP, told The Sun in a statement.

“It’s a disgraceful, deliberate attempt to deceive Iowa voters and manipulate the outcome of these elections,” Cichy said. “Iowans deserve better, and this scheme needs to be called out.”

Our Heritage Matters PAC has also supported libertarian David Graham in Kansas’ U.S. Senate race.

Fellow pop-up super PAC StarkFreedom PAC has joined that effort, but it’s been uniquely transparent about its intentions. Aaron Day, who oversees StarkFreedom PAC, told Semafor this month that he wants to chip away at Republican margins.

Alex DeGrasse, an adviser to incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), told The Sun in a statement that “this is the oldest dark-money trick in [Senate Minority Leader] Chuck Schumer’s playbook.”

“The people behind this scheme aren’t even hiding it anymore,” DeGrasse said.

“It’s deliberate deception, paid for by people who will never reveal their names until after the votes are counted,” he added. “Kansans are smart. They know a vote for anyone but Roger Marshall is a vote for a Schumer majority.”

Concerns of Misrepresentation

Graham, the libertarian, told The Sun in an email that he had “no objection” to outside spending on his behalf, “provided that my views are not misrepresented.”

But PACs The Sun examined have sometimes twisted the beliefs of candidates they’re supporting.

Our Heritage Matters PAC sent mailers to South Carolina voters asking them to vote for libertarian Bill Reeside in the state’s 1st Congressional District. The mailer, a copy of which was shared with The Sun, calls Reeside an “America First Patriot” looking to “end temporary protected status [TPS] for illegal immigrants.”

Reeside told The Sun in a text message that ending temporary protected status is part of his plan, but that the mailer “doesn’t capture my entire plan for fixing our immigration system.”

Likely to the chagrin of MAGA Republicans, Reeside wants to replace temporary protected status and asylum “with unlimited, free work visas for low-skilled workers and high-skilled workers” as well as a “fair path to citizenship for the Dreamers,” according to his website.

Of the Our Heritage Matters advertisement, Reeside said: “I would rate it ‘accurate, but incomplete.’”

While the donations behind Our Heritage Matters are not yet public, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has nudged outside spending groups to emphasize outsider candidates’ conservative bona fides before Election Day, Axios reported.

They’ve done so through a technique known as “redboxing”: sharing talking points on pages of public websites, which does not constitute illegally coordinating with super PACs.

‘Spoiler’ Campaign?

Day, from StarkFreedom PAC, has a firsthand understanding of the strategy: He got almost 18,000 votes in New Hampshire’s 2016 U.S. Senate election, which Republican Kelly Ayotte lost by just over 1,000 votes.

He’s now running a spate of AI-generated ads across the country, looking to replicate that effort.

“You call it a spoiler campaign,” Day told Semafor. “I call it holding Republicans accountable.”

Independent candidate Jay Bowman calls himself “the other guy” in the competitive race to represent Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District.

Bowman supports campaign finance reforms such as ensuring “super PACs are transparent about their donors.”

This hasn’t stopped Our Heritage Matters PAC, which has spent over $130,000 on physical and digital advertising supporting Bowman’s run against Republican Ralph Alvarado and Democrat Zach Dembo.

“They're sowing confusion and trying to take votes away from [the GOP candidate] by promoting an independent candidate, which is too bad,” Bowman said. “I've gotten several angry phone calls, texts … about what's going on, why they're receiving these.”
entries.author: Kyle Chouinard

entries.title: Josh Shapiro Already Sounds Like He’s Running for President
entries.summary: The Pennsylvania governor is getting ready to trounce his opponent on Tuesday. And then…
entries.content:
CAMP HILL, Pa. — It’s easy to forget while listening to Josh Shapiro talk that he doesn’t face Donald Trump on the ballot next week.

During his stump speech here Thursday, the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania — widely seen as a likely 2028 presidential candidate — ripped Trump for bumbling into the Iran war. He mocked the president’s tariffs as economically illiterate. And he denounced Trump’s whole administration as a “chaotic,” “cruel” and “corrupt” mess that has threatened to undo decades of progress.

“The story of our nation has been that in every chapter of our story, it always got better,” Shapiro said at an outdoor rally of a few hundred people, held next to a local Teamsters building. “We’ve always got more free and more just. And I know right now, it feels like we’re in a moment in this chapter where we’ve taken two steps forward — but man oh man, have gotten knocked back a step.”

Drawing on the country’s founding, the governor said that a country created on the bold promise of making life better for people must now reinvigorate that dream.

“This is about doing our part, as Pennsylvanians have for the last 250 years, to be an example to the nation,” Shapiro said. “We stand on the side of freedom. We stand on the side of democracy. We stand on the side of liberty, and we vote that way, we stand that way, and we fight that way.”

He didn’t mention his Republican opponent next week, Stacy Garrity, by name a single time, either in his speech here or during a rally earlier in Schuylkill County.

Shapiro, in an interview with The Washington Sun, said he’s taking nothing for granted in next week’s race, which polls indicate he could win by 20 percentage points or more. And he’s repeatedly dismissed talk of 2028 as premature.

“We don’t want somebody who is going to rubber-stamp whatever Donald Trump wants,” Shapiro said of Garrity. “We want someone who’s going to respect the role of the people. And I think I’ve been very clear about the stark differences between she and I.”

But the Pennsylvania Democrat also has more on the line Tuesday than most governors seeking reelection. Shapiro has invested significant time and resources toward helping four Democratic candidates take on Republican U.S. House incumbents — his rally here Thursday night was held in conjunction with Janelle Stelson, who is running against Rep. Scott Perry in a race viewed as one of 2026’s core battlegrounds.

Shapiro on Thursday was nearing the end of a 29-county, 10-day bus tour across the state, in which he was expected to eventually campaign with all four of the Democratic House candidates.

He’s also trying for a state legislative “trifecta,” giving Democrats majorities in both the Pennsylvania House and Senate for the first time since 1993. Doing so would give the governor a chance to sign into law a legislative wish list that he emphasizes would help the everyday Pennsylvanian.

But it would also give Shapiro a potentially significant platform from which he could launch a presidential campaign. Which, even as the governor denies thinking about it, is evidently on the minds of some of his supporters.

At the event in Schuylkill County, 20-year-old Ayden Rodichok told the governor he’d like to see him run for president. Rodichok was just elected chair of the Schuylkill County Young Democrats and had asked Shapiro to film a short video with him to send to its members.

Shapiro smiled and ignored Rodichok’s suggestion. But the American University student said afterward he really did think it was a good idea, saying the governor could appeal to both progressives and moderates.

“I just said it to be funny, but I would definitely vote for him for president,” Rodichok said.

Shapiro is generally seen as part of an evolving group of leading potential contenders in the 2028 Democratic primary, a list that includes Sen. Jon Ossoff, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

The governor has never lost a statewide general election in his battleground state, winning twice for attorney general and once as a gubernatorial candidate. His electability could be a selling point for some Democratic voters. He’s also seen as more ideologically moderate than other contenders, potentially putting him at odds with some progressives.

Democratic operatives expect that the 2028 Democratic presidential primary could feature two dozen or more candidates, in what some call the most wide-open race in the party’s recent history.

Even as he dismisses questions about a potential presidential run, in the interview, Shapiro acknowledged he talks about Trump because he’s on people’s minds.

“There are a lot of people who are showing up because they're scared about the direction our country’s heading in,” he said. They're angry about it. They want to do something to channel that anger, that fear, that concern, into action.”

During his speech here, Shapiro highlighted ways in which his administration had successfully stood up to the White House, including on voting rights and ICE detention centers. He also outlined how, with the help of a Democratic-held House and Senate, he would raise the minimum wage to $15, invest in housing construction and codify abortion-rights protections.

If he gets another four years as governor, Shapiro pledged he would think about nothing other than how to help Pennsylvanians — and how to keep pushing back against Trump.

“The other thing I'm thinking about,” he said, “is how to fight back against this chaos, how to stand up against the cruelty and how not to tolerate his corruption in America any longer.”
entries.author: Alex Roarty

entries.title: A World Series That Reminded Us Just How Good Baseball Can Be
entries.summary: The Brewers-Rays showdown was a shining example of a sport that, at its best and most decent, gives so much to so many.
entries.content:
For six days, my friends and I texted, talked and e-mailed about how much we were enjoying the World Series. People whom I’d call general fans, as well as us MLB nuts, said, “Great! Fun game. I watched every pitch.”

When it ended with Game 5, all of us, except two happy folks from Milwaukee, said, “Sorry it’s over. I wanted it to go seven.”

What was so appealing about this World Series? Why did it feel like a kind of balm, a nightly therapy, to us and to millions more, too? Even now, why do we love a parade in Milwaukee on Halloween?

Much of it was simply superb baseball, properly played, with all aspects of the sport on display in pleasing proportions.

But with time, I suspect some of us will also see this World Series as a bit of a barely veiled morality play about civility; mutual respect between franchises of modest means; stars with humility; teams that can't afford gold toilet seats in their clubhouses; and unselfish team play rather than Me First.

Whatever the combination, the public was ready for it. TV ratings for the Brewers’ five-game win over the Tampa Bay Rays blew far past (low) expectations and rose to the level of well-loved, larger-market World Series of the past. Everybody is happy except for Fox, which, after 14.22 million viewers for Game 5, lusted for the fat numbers that would have accompanied a Game 6 and 7.

The “critical consensus” is that fans loved the competitive balance of seeing the clubs with the 19th- and 28th-ranked payrolls (Milwaukee and Tampa Bay, respectively) finish with the best records in their leagues, then not only beat but sweep the big-bucks bullies. The Rays skunked the Yankees three straight in the ALDS and the Brewers flattened the aging, stunned Dodgers in four games in the NLCS.

Even better, both the new-champ Brewers and the Rays value every aspect of the sport, honoring all of the last 125 years. They aren’t one-dimensional modern teams that, to exaggerate, “swing hard in case you hit it.”

Both teams seek mastery of every facet: steals, hit-and-runs, contact hitting as well as power swings, 100-mph fastballs, bunts, crazy-deep bullpens, acrobatic defense and analytics.

In five games, there were 14 steals, perhaps 20 bunt attempts, but only four homers.

“There hasn’t been a bunt in the last five World Series,” grinned MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred.

But something else important ran through this World Series.

This contest brought us six days of civility.

In the midst of fierce competition, there was respect for the game and mutual respect among all the players without any exceptions.

That civility and dignity, honoring something of value — like a franchise winning its first World Series — extended to the towns that wanted the same prize, desperately.
Brewers (2428x1773, AR: 1.37)Brewer fans almost equaled the noise of Rays fans in Tampa Bay games. “Altercations?” This ain’t Philly, the Fenway or Yankee Stadium bleachers, or the Dodger parking lot. Brewer and Rays fans sat next to each other and … cheered. (Or laughed. Or maybe prayed.)

Not one player bragged in a TV interview, except to brag on a teammate. In the entire postseason, the only brief show of bravado was the Rays’ young star Junior Caminero mimicking a broom sweep after dispatching the Yankees.

The biggest star-power name in the Series was the modest, almost shy Jacob Misiorowski, whom manager Pat Murphy nicknamed “Forest Gump.” After a 15-strikeout win this year, The Miz posted an AI-generated photo of his head on Gump’s body, sitting on that park bench.

After getting two Series wins with a 0.84 ERA but “only” going 10⅔

innings in those starts, Miz deflected questions about himself and talked about the joy of fans back in Milwaukee, until he started to tear up.

Brewers manager Murphy, after Milwaukee lost Game 4 in 12 innings after being three outs away from a championship, could have been Belichick-brusque. Instead, he was generous, calm and honest. “This is going to be hard,” he said. “They’ve very good. But winning a world title is supposed to be hard.”

Only once, in five games, did tensions appear to rise, when two players had a brief staredown at home plate. In the 11th inning of Game 4, catcher William Contreras challenged a “ball’’ call on the Rays’ Yandy Diaz (and his 20-inch biceps). As the pair awaited the ruling, they — maybe the toughest customers on each team — locked eyes, their faces a foot apart.

The “moment” went viral. But not because they were angry; rather, in MLB, most staredowns are mock-serious. This time, Contreras was wrong on his challenge. That broke the stare; Contreras gave a little smirk, called the next pitch — and won Series MVP.

Not once did a player on either team criticize a player from the other club. There was no online snark or trolling.

With hindsight, this Series could, in a parallel universe — but not, thankfully, the MLB universe — have been filled with noxious controversy and even conspiracy theory.

In Game 1, the Brewers celebrated what they thought was a game-ending double play. They were into postgame rejoicing. But the Rays challenged, claiming pivot man Cooper Pratt’s foot might have left the second-base bag — by an inch — before securing the ball.

Everyone watched the scoreboard. Would the Brewers win the game? Or would the game continue with Rays at second and third base, trailing 3-2 — in other words, a mere two-run single away from taking the lead. Triple gulp.

Emotionally, psychologically, would Milwaukee have to win twice within minutes?

Minutes passed as about 30 people in the 900-square-foot MLB Replay Operations Center in New York (“The Rock”) collaborated, including an umpire supervisor, a technical captain and two MLB umpires. If the Rays came back to win, that call would flip a Series game, and thus switch which team, based on history, would have a 64 percent chance to win it all.

Some joked about one person alone in a small dark room somewhere making the decision. That’s catchier than a lot of competent people trying to make a hard decision correctly.

The Rays won the challenge. But the Brewers escaped when reliever Trevor Megill composed himself and fanned the final hitter.

“They handled that decision the right way,” Murphy said. “If the Rays had come back to win, I’d say the same thing.”

Everybody in MLB knows he would’ve.

The very next night, Game 2 ended on a controversial checked-swing third strike against Diaz. There’s no replay for that call (yet). It’s the umpire’s judgment. Diaz threw up his hands.

But that was it.

Nobody on either team, either night, challenged the integrity or motives of anybody involved. Everybody respected the difficulty of the decisions that had to be made.

Everyone said, “That’s baseball.” Because that is baseball. You do everything possible to get things right. Then live with it. That’s as fair as life gets; which isn’t 100 percent. If you can’t cope with that deal, then MLB will eat you up.

“We was robbed” is probably older than the Bible. But in the real world of contemporary sports, you almost never hear such sour grapes. Those, especially in leadership positions, who blame the refs or the breaks seldom last long. At least in sports, everybody sees through a loser.

You never deny the result once all the proper processes have been applied. That would steal credit from your opponent; few things in MLB are more dishonorable. No one disgraces himself by saying, “I didn’t really lose.”

MLB has plenty of flaws. But none that big.

Now, the show is over. In its place, the “business of baseball” slinks on next. No wonder I hate irony.

After this World Series, we’re a month or so from a lockout by the owners. Let’s hold the vitriol, against both sides perhaps, for a little while — and let the Brewers, so often tricked over the last 56 years, enjoy their mammoth treat.

For now, cling to this World Series between two small-market teams that were good-to-exceptional at every phase of the game, using each element in its appropriate moment.

Let us hope that everyone in the game remembers this interlude where civility and thrills, intelligence and jubilation, modesty and pride could coexist and do everyone credit.

Then, when the billions are stacked high on the bargaining table, maybe they’ll try to do as little damage as possible to a game that, at its best and most decent, gives so much to so many.
entries.author: Thomas Boswell

entries.title: Austin Ekeler Has a Media Future Ahead of Him. But Football Is First.
entries.summary: The Commanders running back and longtime fantasy football star has appeared on Netflix and regularly posts videos on his social media accounts.
entries.content:
There are any number of reasons why NFL players jump into the sports media world both during and after their playing careers.

Perhaps they view it as a way to stay connected to the sport. It may be that they are motivated to dominate another profession after they’re done playing.

When it comes to Commanders running back Austin Ekeler, one of his forays into sports media was simply due to boredom.

“My Achilles was torn, so I'm not any use on the field,” Ekeler said of his stint as a pregame analyst for Netflix during the Christmas Day broadcast of Commanders-Cowboys last season. “So hey, here's an opportunity to go and talk about my team in a positive way here on a cool stage.”

The Netflix game was one of many instances where Ekeler has found himself in front of a camera sans helmet, pads and cleats. Throughout his 10-year career, Ekeler has been one of the most productive third-down running backs in the NFL: His 4,318 receiving yards since 2017 are the third-most by a running back in that time span.

But the 31-year-old, coming off a torn Achilles suffered last season in Week 2, is nearing the end of his career. As Ekeler contemplates what’s next, he’s positioning himself in the worlds of business, technology and — most notably — sports media.

He hasn’t yet decided exactly what he wants the next stage of his life to look like — he’s still trying to help get the 1-4-1 Commanders back to the playoffs this season — but Ekeler knows he has the basic skills to end up on your favorite sports channel.

“I don't know if I'm good on camera, but I speak with confidence, and I have opinions on some things, and I express that,” he said.

But the story of Ekeler’s broadcasting aspirations doesn’t start in a journalism classroom or a production studio. It starts in fantasy sports.

After years of running fantasy football leagues — and as one of the top-performing fantasy running backs in the NFL — Ekeler founded his own free fantasy platform, Fantasy Royale, while recovering from Achilles surgery last year. The 12,000-user website and app is focused on building a community of the best fantasy players in the country.

To market and drive users to Fantasy Royale, he leveraged the social equity he’d built up with his nearly 560,000 followers across Instagram, Threads, X, Facebook, TikTok and Linkedin through shortform videos giving analysis on individual player performances. The videos showcase both his natural charisma and his understanding of the social media landscape — which requires posting content that people want to engage with on a consistent basis.

“That's what our world is nowadays. It's a blessing and a curse,” Ekeler said. “Because if you can hit the algorithms well, boom, it's free marketing. If you can't, you're gonna get buried by everyone else.”

For years Ekeler has been told he should go into broadcasting following his NFL career. While he’s intrigued by the idea, it would have to be in a role that matches his positive personality and philosophy. The hot-take debate style of modern sports media doesn't appeal to him — and neither does the toxicity that can be aimed at players from sports bettors or fantasy players upset over their performances.

“I just don't want to be in the light talking about guys in a negative way even though that might be the situation,” he said.

Ekeler recognizes, however, that the broadcasting industry gives him the opportunity to spotlight the players who aren’t household names. Ekeler went from an undrafted rookie out of Division II Western Colorado to an All-Pro selection.

“The positive side about it is you do get to share with the world these players that are coming up, share the journey,” he said. “We need the stories to be told.”

To better prepare himself for media work, Ekeler has attended the broadcasting bootcamp the NFL puts on annually for former players, including current player-turned-analyst Jason Kelce (ESPN). A talent evaluator from the program regularly messages Ekeler notes when watching him in postgame press conferences.

Immediate feedback like that is the closest the media profession compares to football, Ekeler said. After a game or practice, players can watch film and speak with their coaches about where they excelled and where they can improve for the next game.

It’s the same for broadcasting. You can rewatch segments and speak with producers immediately after stepping off set, allowing you to adjust before your next appearance.

“If you can get [feedback] all the time and often, it's amazing because you're going to continue to make strides, and your standard of what good is is going to continue to get better,” Ekeler said.

But football is not over yet. Ekeler missed the rest of the 2025 season with Washington (who he signed with in 2024) recovering from the torn Achilles. Up until a few months ago, he didn’t feel like he was ready to return to the field. He’d watch film of his training sessions and not recognize the former fantasy football stud. He thought his career was over.

“I'm 31. Age is undefeated,” Ekeler said in late September. “I'm grandpa in the running back room.”

But as time went on, he felt he had more left in the tank. Ekeler re-signed with the team on Sept. 29 and immediately debuted with the team on Oct. 4 in London.

He made an immediate splash after over a year off: four carries for 29 yards (7.3 yards per carry) and one reception for 11 yards. But his usage has slipped in the two games since, playing just 10% of snaps against the Giants and 49ers. While learning a new playbook is “like learning a new language,” Ekeler said the fundamentals are all the same. A wide zone or gap scheme is the same across all playbooks. Because of the volume of plays — and the new terminology — it’s taken Ekeler a few weeks to memorize things, but he feels comfortable now.

With more time — and starter Bill Croskey-Merritt on injured reserve for the next three games — head coach Dan Quinn said he expects Ekeler’s workload to pick up.

“I feel his quickness, I feel his decisiveness,” Quinn said. “So now that he's back, we'll need to lean in more, and he's able to handle a bigger workload now.

Ekeler is interested in one day being on television, but as Washington fights to keep its slim playoff hopes alive, he’s more concerned about his day job.

“I like those types of opportunities because it's a one and done,” he said of the Netflix job. “I'm not ready to go full on broadcaster because … it's homework nonstop, knowing stories, keeping up. I'm not ready for that yet.”
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Wizards Beat Hornets, 95-79, in AJ Dybantsa's Home Debut
entries.summary: The rookie scored 17 points and Washington's defense smothered Charlotte's offense in a decisive win.
entries.content:
Trae Young had 21 points, nine assists and seven rebounds, AJ Dybantsa scored 17 points in his home debut, and the Washington Wizards routed the Charlotte Hornets 95-79 on Friday night.

Washington held the Hornets to 13 points in the third quarter, cruising to a comfortable victory on the first night of NBA Cup play. Anthony Davis had 25 points and 13 rebounds for the Wizards.

Dybantsa wasn’t available to start the season because of an ankle injury, but this year’s No. 1 overall draft pick finally played Wednesday night, scoring 19 points in a loss at Cleveland. He looked composed again Friday in front of the home fans. Dybantsa had an impressive putback in the fourth quarter negated by a basket interference call. A short while later, he switched hands while driving before banking in a shot while being fouled.

That drew an “MVP! MVP!” chant for the 19-year-old rookie.

The story of this game, however, was Charlotte’s atrocious shooting. The Hornets led by 10 in the first quarter after starting 4 of 10 from 3-point range. Then they made four of their next 29 attempts from long range.

Charlotte ended up shooting 29.7% from the field for the game, 12 of 56 from 3-point range. The Hornets are now responsible for the two lowest-scoring games in the NBA this season, having produced 81 points in an Oct. 23 loss to Atlanta.

Brandon Miller led the Hornets with 19 points. Naz Reid was back in the starting lineup for Charlotte after being benched in the second half at Detroit on Wednesday night. Reid had 12 points and 11 rebounds.

The Hornets have been without Kon Knueppel (hamstring) and Coby White (calf) all season so far. Grant Williams (hamstring) has also been out.

Up Next

Wizards: At Orlando on Monday night.

entries.title: D.C., Virginia Sue Trump Adminstration Over Proposed Triumphal Arch
entries.summary: The lawsuit from the D.C. and Virginia attorneys general joins a growing collection of legal challenges to the 250-foot tall structure.
entries.content:
D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones are suing the Trump administration over the president’s proposed triumphal arch, seeking to block its construction by arguing that the project is not authorized by Congress and violates the District’s building height restrictions.

The lawsuit, filed Saturday, joins a growing collection of legal challenges to the 250-foot tall structure. Officials in Arlington County have also sued the Trump administration over the arch, arguing the government had failed to complete a mandatory environmental review. A group of Vietnam War veterans filed a lawsuit in February, arguing it would impede on the nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

The D.C. and Virginia attorneys general also argue that construction of the arch will “snarl traffic,” pollute the Potomac River, disrupt emergency services and pose other challenges for their jurisdictions – and allege that the Trump administration has made only “half-hearted gestures” at complying with laws that require careful review of ambitious construction projects in the District.

“This project is flagrantly unlawful,” said the complaint from D.C. and Virginia. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

The matter is time-sensitive. Trump administration lawyers have said they hope to proceed quickly with construction, and a federal review panel stacked with Trump appointees could approve designs for the arch as soon as Nov. 5.

The war veterans suing Trump are also asking U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan to block the project before Nov. 4. Chutkan heard arguments in the case on Friday.

Trump first proposed the arch last year as a triumphant structure to mark the country’s 250th anniversary. But recently, in the face of several legal challenges, the administration has unveiled a new, national-security focused argument in favor of the arch. In legal filings this week, Trump officials said the arch could help protect the country against coordinated drone attacks — though initial plans published by the National Capital Planning Commission did not mention national security.

The arch is one of several projects Trump has undertaken to reshape the city’s facade in his image. The administration has removed hundreds of trees from East Potomac Park as it seeks to transform the city’s East Potomac Golf Links into a “world class championship” course, drawing fears from locals about the destruction of a beloved and publicly-accessible community destination.

Trump has also embarked on a significant renovation of the Kennedy Center, even adding his name to the building before a federal judge forced the administration to remove it.

Saturday’s lawsuit is one of several that Schwalb has filed against the Trump administration this term. The attorney general’s office is fighting the National Guard deployment in court, and also successfully sued to block Trump’s attempt to sidestep the city’s police chief and install his own police commissioner in the District.
entries.author: Jenny Gathright
